findings.where: Article specimen, the photograph's caption and the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?' below it, at desktop and phone
findings.fault: The subhead sits right against the caption, with no space above it. Elsewhere a subhead gets more space above than below. Here it has almost none above and a full gap below, so it reads as part of the caption block, not as the start of a new section.
findings.who_objects: Angélique and the founder. The brief asks this specimen to prove that the type rhythm holds when an image, caption and subhead are added. It shows the opposite at exactly that join, and a reader of Mark's article loses where the new section starts.

findings.where: Article specimen, the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?' compared with the article title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law', worst on phone
findings.fault: The subhead is set at least as large and heavy as the article title. On phone it is clearly larger: about 38 px against the title's 32. The section heading outranks the page title.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank reader skimming one of Mark's articles. The size order tells them the mid-article subhead is the page's main heading. The founder would object too, because the specimen is meant to set the template that every article inherits.

findings.where: Article specimen, the three-item bulleted list and the hairline and related-lecture link straight after it, at desktop and phone
findings.fault: The list items are set almost solid, with far tighter line spacing than the 19/30 paragraphs just above them. Wrapped items such as 'a series of chapters… Cycle.' and 'Coordination and Responsibilities; and' crowd together. The last line then runs straight into the hairline, with no space below the list.
findings.who_objects: Angélique, who will add lists to Mark's articles, and any reader. The list looks cramped and like a different text from the body around it, which is the hand-tuned, broken rhythm that round 1's critics asked this round to rule out.

findings.where: First screen, the giant ghost 'PPP' letters behind Mark's heading (on phone, a cropped 'PP' fragment beside the heading)
findings.fault: A second, enormous layer of display serif letters sits under the heading. The heading's own letters cross over its stems and bowls, so the two serif layers tangle and the line loses its clean edge. On phone the cropped 'PP' reads as a stray mark, not as letters.
findings.who_objects: A visitor reading Mark's one large line, and the founder. The research asks for one very large serif line, using scale contrast rather than more elements, and this adds a competing type element right behind it. The founder would also see a decorative device that any consultancy could use.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'The World's Best…' against the subhead's ‘chapter topics’ and the curly quotes in the body
findings.fault: The title's apostrophe is a straight or prime-like mark. The subhead and body use true curly quotation marks. Like marks are not set alike, and the straight one stands out at display size.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader in law and policy who is used to well-set documents. At headline size the odd mark looks careless on a page that is meant to signal the gravitas of a legal journal.
